prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of GLP-1 physiology and the development of incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us ranked B006 first, and I do not treat that agreement as the argument. The argument is the chain itself. Holst's work on the incretin effect and GLP-1 secretion in humans, and Drucker's work on GLP-1 and GLP-2 receptor biology and tissue actions, define a physiological axis. Long-acting analogues then turned that axis into drugs. The mechanisms (glucose-dependent insulin secretion, appetite and gastric effects) have been confirmed independently for decades. Large randomized outcome trials now show cardiovascular and renal benefit alongside metabolic benefit. Few discoveries combine this much mechanistic clarity with this much clinical consequence, and delaying recognition further has no scientific justification. Including Knudsen lets the prize honour the step that made the class usable, which was the albumin-binding acylation that gave liraglutide and semaglutide their durable action. It also keeps the prize to the three-person limit.
statement.case_against: The credit allocation is the real weakness. Four of the six openings, including mine, differ on the third name, and this is not a cosmetic point. Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) form is a decisive early step, and Habener, who is not in the supplied names, is part of that record. A prize with Knudsen risks being read as favouring industrial drug design over discovery. A prize without her ignores the step that made the therapy possible. There is also a case that the prize would be recognising three different kinds of work (physiology, peptide chemistry and drug engineering) under one heading. I have not resolved whether that is one achievement or several.

responses.point: Perlmann argues that Drucker, Holst and Mojsov are the most defensible trio, because Mojsov's identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is a discovery contribution. He regards Knudsen's role as industrial development, which is distinct from discovery. He also ranks B039 (the unfolded protein response, Mori and Walter) a clean second.
responses.response: I take the Mojsov point seriously, and I agree the active-peptide identification was necessary. I still weigh it differently. Identifying the peptide and showing its activity was necessary, but without the acylated analogues there is no drug class, and the prize is for a change in medicine as well as for a hormone. On the structure of the prize, however, I agree with you that B039 is the cleanest candidate on the list: two people, a defined mechanism, no real credit dispute. I would put it as my first alternative. Our disagreement over the third name in B006 comes down to whether the prize's weight sits on discovery or on translation. I have not settled that, and I would want to see the evidence on Mojsov's contribution to the original sequence and activity work set against Knudsen's design papers before the final ballot.

responses.point: The chair also proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen and describes the discovery-to-drug arc as rare. He admits that credit is spread across several groups and that no three-person set can include everyone. He also ranks the HPV vaccine (B035) fourth.
responses.response: We agree on the trio, but agreement between two of us does not settle the attribution problem, and I do not want the committee to treat it as settled. If the chair's reasoning for Knudsen is that translation deserves a place, then the committee should state that principle openly, because it then also bears on B004 and B040, where industrial and clinical development are mixed with discovery. On B035 I am less persuaded than you that it should rank above the cGAS-STING pathway. Its impact is concrete and mature, but the credit problem with Zhou Jian, who has died and is not on the list, makes a three-name configuration hard to defend.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks B006 first with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov and treats a split between basic science and drug development as a possibility. He leans toward the basic-science side. He ranks B039 second and B004 third.
responses.response: Your split between basic science and drug development is the right framing, and your preference for the former is a fair position, though I do not share it fully. Where we agree is that B039 deserves serious weight. My reservation about B004 is the one you identify yourself: the attribution is cut by the omission of Eshhar, so any trio for B004 draws a line that will be criticised. I would not put B004 ahead of B006 on that ground. I would keep it as a second alternative because its core achievement, durable remissions in refractory B-cell malignancies, is mature.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks B006 first with Mojsov and places cGAS-STING (B028) third, with Chen and Barber as a clean two-person attribution. She notes that therapeutic translation of STING agonists has been disappointing.
responses.response: I agree that Chen and Barber is a clean pair and that the mechanism is well confirmed. I am more cautious than you about timing. If the justification rests on mechanism alone, then its relevance to autoimmunity, infection and cancer immunity is mostly inferred, and the therapeutic record you describe does not yet support it. I would keep B028 behind B039 on maturity of clinical and physiological consequence. I would not put it ahead of B037 on methodological impact.

uncertainties: Who among Holst, Drucker, Mojsov, Knudsen and Habener should be credited, and whether the prize should reward physiology, peptide chemistry or drug development, or all three.
Whether the committee can justify a prize that includes industrial drug design without applying the same standard consistently to other shortlisted candidates.
I rely on my own recollection of the GLP-1 record rather than a verified primary-literature check, so the claims about early peptide priority are uncertain.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B006, B039 or B004. My documented connections (a 2019 review with Sten Grillner, work with Patrik Ernfors, and a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann) concern motor-circuit neuroscience and stem-cell-derived neurons, and none of them involves a shortlisted candidate. B037 (optogenetics) is in my own field of neuroscience, but I list no personal tie to its candidates.
